tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: Windows PowerShell 5.1 (powershell.exe)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` are NOT available — they cause a parser error. To run B only if A succeeds: `A; if ($?) { B }`. To chain unconditionally: `A; B`.
   - Ternary (`?:`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are NOT available. Use `if/else` and explicit `$null -eq` checks instead.
   - Avoid `2>&1` on native executables. In 5.1, redirecting a native command's stderr inside PowerShell wraps each line in an ErrorRecord (NativeCommandError) and sets `$?` to `$false` even when the exe returned exit code 0. stderr is already captured for you — don't redirect it.
   - `>`, `>>`, and `Out-File` usually default to UTF-8 (with BOM) in this environment, but `Set-Content`/`Add-Content` still default to the system ANSI codepage — when writing a file other tools will read, pass `-Encoding utf8` explicitly to `Out-File`/`Set-Content`.
   - `ConvertFrom-Json` returns a PSCustomObject, not a hashtable. `-AsHashtable` is not available.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

A workflow size guideline is configured for this session: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale.

`<operator_authored>
# What this list is

These are the core components of the harness that must be prioritized to establish a system that can faithfully support future work. Until a suitable solution to all of this list is implemented, all additions to this harness must be in service to one of these components. 

**They don't need to be built linearly, nor in the exact order listed below**.

1. **Task specification and definition of done**. Acceptance criteria are set before work starts. Each task is scoped to the operator's capacity that day: a smaller scope at full precision, rather than the same scope at lower precision.
2. **Boot context and standing instructions**. A way to manage what the assistant loads at session start and what it loads only on a trigger. Also a few key lines in instruction files that the community broadly agrees improve assistant behaviour.
3. **Delegation**. Subagents, choosing model and effort, parallel sessions, and git worktrees.
4. **Permissions and safety boundaries**. What the assistant may do without asking, and what needs the operator's approval.
5. **Capability discovery**. A map of available skills, from the Anthropic marketplace or reputable repos. For each skill, it gives the conditions where invoking it would improve the output compared with relying on the assistant's default training data.
6. **Verification methods and their triggers**. A list of verification methods, with the trigger for when each one is used.
7. **Operator legibility**. How an operator who isn't a software engineer sees what was done and what code is running.
8. **Session handover.** A handover protocol between sessions that supports any number of multi-session tasks.
9. **Building on proven practice**. A reliable way to build on the converged wisdom of practitioners more skilled than the operator, so that builds start from a solid foundation. It works as a fixed step at the start of every build: look outside first, then choose to adopt, adap
10. **Knowledge storage and retrieval**. A way to store the findings of earlier research and retrieve them at the momthey are needed.
11. **Evaluating a change**. Evaluations of why an approach worked and why an approach didn't. This is separate from verification, which asks whether one out whether a change improved outcomes, whichneeds a baseline taken before the change.
12. **Pruning**. Retiring instructions and toolselves.
13. **Scheduling and unattended runs**. Running work on a schedule or without the operator present.

## How to reference this list

When referring to an item on this list, do not refer to it by it's number (e.g. This supports core component #3). Instead, refer to each using the bolded string in each item on the list (e.g. this supports **Knowledge storage and retrieval**)

## Disambiguation of terms

The core components of the harness, outlined in this document, are not the same as System Components, which is a controlled vocabulary and which refers to something else.

 A key design constraint to consider is that the operator often has low energy and focus. He understands the level of intent needed to communicate to the assistant to get the outcomes he wants, but often struggles to overcome the friction and effort requirements to do so. 

## Key operator failure mode

The most frequent and damaging failure mode is initiating complex tasks regardless of his inability to overcome the effort requirements to communicate his intent is sufficient detail.

### Implication

The Core Privatives (see controlled vocabulary) are an experimental attempt to provide a low friction pipeline to lower the effort threshold of communicating his intent at the level needed to get the standard of output he seeks on complex tasks.

## Don'ts

- Never edit the problem file. It is operator-authored.
- Never implement in this run, even if the fix looks small.
- Never mark a spec approved without the operator's answer to the gate.

So I need a workflow that allows for legibility by any given recommendation or repeating back my intent to being simple enough to fall within my effort theshold, and to allow for corrections that also fall within that threshold. The process must also not vary in efficacy whether I complete the pipeline in one sitting, or choose to pause at any point and continue later. content.text:
Here's the framework as I understand it, numbered so you can correct by number.

**The core constraint**
1. **Effort is capped by rate, not total.** Your working memory ("RAM") is small, but the total effort over time isn't capped. Every single step has to fit in RAM.
2. **The target is parity** with what has worked before: heavy up-front intent clarification, then a one-shot build. That method works, but its up-front step is now beyond your threshold.
3. **Small steps must not lose anything.** Splitting the work into RAM-sized pieces must not drop intent compared with doing it all up front.

**Approaches already ruled out (you've tried them)**
4. **Less intent, hoping newer models fill the gaps.** Result: processes you can't read, skipped verification, unusable outputs, broken pipelines.
5. **Interview → report.** You never read it, and you can't check its quality or precision.
6. **Interview → document of verbatim questions and answers.**
   - (a) It isn't pulled up when the model actually makes a decision.
   - (b) It gets over-generalized, causing second-order effects that end up net negative.

**What the new pipeline must do**
7. **Legible at each step.** Every recommendation, or restatement of your intent, is simple enough to check within your threshold.
8. **Cheap corrections.** Fixing a misread also fits within your threshold.
9. **Pausing doesn't matter.** Results are the same whether you finish in one sitting or stop anywhere and resume later.
10. **It surfaces unknown unknowns.** That means questions you didn't know to ask, and proven methods you didn't know existed, often findable with a simple external search.

**Implied, my inference (confirm or strike):**
- **From 6a/6b:** captured intent has to be tied to the specific decision it governs, and come up at that decision. Its scope should stay as narrow as what you actually said.
- **From 9:** all pipeline state lives in files, never only in session context.

**Two tensions I can already see:**
- **10 vs 1.** Bringing up unknown unknowns adds new material, and new material uses RAM. Whatever does the surfacing has to filter hard before it reaches you.
- **3 vs 9.** Each pause is a point where intent can leak. The file state has to carry intent through a pause, not just progress.

Correct anything by number, then send me your ideas and I'll take the adversarial pass.

content.content:
# Controlled vocabulary

The terms the harness uses with one fixed meaning. When a term here is used, it means exactly this and nothing looser. Entries are listed alphabetically.

## INDEX

> **Temporary home.** This entry is a file-tree convention rather than vocabulary, and will move once a better place for it exists. It sits here because there is none yet.

`INDEX.md` catalogues a directory of files: one line per file saying what it is and when to read it. A directory that holds subdirectories gets a `ROUTING_<DIR>` file instead.

## Intake Primitives

The three kinds of item the operator drops into the harness for later processing: **questions**, **ideas** and **problems**. Each has the same structure and is handled by the same `/sweep` skill.

**Operator only.** Only the operator creates Intake Primitives. The assistant never writes a question, idea or problem into a `_New` file, never ticks a ready box, and never adds an item to a backlog itself. It only sweeps the operator's items and, later, processes them.

| Primitive | Prefix | Lives in | Leads to |
|---|---|---|---|
| Question | `QUES_` | `Knowledge/Questions/` | Research, then knowledge base entries. |
| Idea | `IDEA_` | `Work/Ideas/` | A spec, then completed deliverables (e.g. client work), or workflows that produce deliverables. |
| Problem | `PROB_` | `System/Problems/` | Something in the harness that needs improving or adding, then a build-out spec, then implementation. |

The workflows that carry each primitive from backlog to its end point are not designed yet.

**Problem or Idea?** Problems add functionality to the harness itself. Ideas add pipelines that produce outputs which leave the harness. The boundary is fuzzy, and the two may later collapse into a single primitive.

Each Intake Primitive has three folders, named `<prefix>New`, `<prefix>Backlog` and `<prefix>Processed`:
- `_New` holds 10 blank files copied from a template (`TEMPLATE_QUESTIONS.md`, `TEMPLATE_IDEAS.md`, `TEMPLATE_PROBLEMS.md`). The operator writes inside the fence and ticks the ready box.
- `_Backlog` holds ready items, moved there by `/sweep` and named `<prefix><YYYY-MM-DD>_<HHMMSS>.md`.
- `_Processed` holds items a later workflow has dealt with. `/sweep` never touches it.

Unticked files that hold text stay in `_New`, renamed `<prefix>Incomplete_NN.md`.

## ROUTING_<DIR>

> **Temporary home.** This entry is a file-tree convention rather than vocabulary, and will move once a better place for it exists. It sits here because there is none yet.

`ROUTING_<DIR>.md` routes a directory of subdirectories: one entry per subdirectory saying what it holds and when to go there. `<DIR>` is the directory's name in capitals (`ROUTING_SYSTEM.md` in `System/`); the harness root's is `ROUTING_ROOT.md`. A directory that holds files gets an `INDEX` instead.

`ROUTING_ROOT.md` is pointed to only by the parent working directory, which uses it to manage the proper functioning of all System Components. System Components do not route through it.

## System Components

The child working directories that sit side by side at the harness root. Each has its own role and owns a set of system responsibilities that no other System Component shares. Each has its own `CLAUDE.md` for boot context, its own local skills, and a reading list drawing on both its own files and the parent's.

A System Component's fence is the smallest amount of access to the rest of the system it needs to carry out its responsibilities. It gets no more than that.

| System Component | Role |
|---|---|
| `Knowledge/` | Research and knowledge bases. Manages the Questions pipeline. |
| `Work/` | Creating outputs meant for external use. Manages the Ideas pipeline. |

`System/` is not a System Component. It is the parent directory's own file tree, has no `CLAUDE.md`, and is not a working directory.
#####
# System Information index

- Controlled vocabulary.md - the terms the harness uses with one fixed meaning (e.g. INDEX, Intake Primitives, ROUTING_<DIR>, System Components). Read when a term in an instruction file or from the operator might be a defined term, or before naming a new kind of thing.
#####

**1. Framework**

```markdown
# Question pipeline: design framework

## Goal
Approach parity with the efficacy of heavy frontloaded intent clarification followed by a one-shot approach, using a pipeline that stays within Operator RAM.

## Constraint
Effort is capped by rate, not total. Each step along the pipeline must fit within Operator RAM, and must not become lossy by being broken up into small steps.

## Ruled out (tried, non-viable)
- **Less intent, hoping the model fills the gap:** processes not legible to the operator, no proper verification steps, unusable outputs, broken pipelines.
- **Interview → report:** never read; no verification of its quality or precision.
- **Interview → Q&A document of verbatim quotes:** not retrieved when the model makes decisions, or over-generalized into net-negative second-order effects.

## Requirements
1. **Legible:** every recommendation, or repeating back of the operator's intent, is simple enough to fall within Operator RAM.
2. **Correctable:** corrections also fall within Operator RAM.
3. **Pause-proof:** efficacy does not vary between completing the pipeline in one sitting and pausing at any point to continue later. Pipeline state lives in files, not in the session.
4. **Reveals unknown unknowns:** the questions the operator doesn't know to ask, and the proven methodologies available to him, often found by simple external search.
5. **Retrieved at the decision:** captured intent comes up when the decision it governs is made, and its scope stays no wider than the operator stated.
```

**2. Controlled vocabulary entry**

```markdown
## Operator RAM

The operator's capacity for concurrent effort: how much intent, context and decision-making he can hold at one time. It caps the rate of effort, not the total; total effort over time is not capped. A step fits within Operator RAM when the operator can read, check and correct it on its own, without holding other steps in mind.
```

# Lexicon

Provisional names: terms that came to mind in the moment to convey an idea, not yet settled as the official way to describe it. A term may later be rephrased while carrying the same meaning, and an entry may list sibling aliases that carry that meaning. An entry with no sibling aliases is still the current default way to refer to its concept. Once a name settles, its entry moves to the Controlled vocabulary. Entries are listed alphabetically.

## Operator RAM

The operator's capacity for concurrent effort: how much intent, context and decision-making he can hold at one time. It caps the rate of effort, not the total; total effort over time is not capped. A step fits within Operator RAM when the operator can read, check and correct it on its own, without holding other steps in mind.

**Aliases:** none.

# Controlled vocabulary

The terms the harness uses with one fixed meaning. When a term here is used, it means exactly this and nothing looser. Entries are listed alphabetically.

## INDEX

> **Temporary home.** This entry is a file-tree convention rather than vocabulary, and will move once a better place for it exists. It sits here because there is none yet.

`INDEX.md` catalogues a directory of files: one line per file saying what it is and when to read it. A directory that holds subdirectories gets a `ROUTING_<DIR>` file instead.

## Intake Primitives

The three kinds of item the operator drops into the harness for later processing: **questions**, **ideas** and **problems**. Each has the same structure and is handled by the same `/sweep` skill.

**Operator only.** Only the operator creates Intake Primitives. The assistant never writes a question, idea or problem into a `_New` file, never ticks a ready box, and never adds an item to a backlog itself. It only sweeps the operator's items and, later, processes them.

| Primitive | Prefix | Lives in | Leads to |
|---|---|---|---|
| Question | `QUES_` | `Knowledge/Questions/` | Research, then knowledge base entries. |
| Idea | `IDEA_` | `Work/Ideas/` | A spec, then completed deliverables (e.g. client work), or workflows that produce deliverables. |
| Problem | `PROB_` | `System/Problems/` | Something in the harness that needs improving or adding, then a build-out spec, then implementation. |

The workflows that carry each primitive from backlog to its end point are not designed yet.

**Problem or Idea?** Problems add functionality to the harness itself. Ideas add pipelines that produce outputs which leave the harness. The boundary is fuzzy, and the two may later collapse into a single primitive.

Each Intake Primitive has three folders, named `<prefix>New`, `<prefix>Backlog` and `<prefix>Processed`:
- `_New` holds 10 blank files copied from a template (`TEMPLATE_QUESTIONS.md`, `TEMPLATE_IDEAS.md`, `TEMPLATE_PROBLEMS.md`). The operator writes inside the fence and ticks the ready box.
- `_Backlog` holds ready items, moved there by `/sweep` and named `<prefix><YYYY-MM-DD>_<HHMMSS>.md`.
- `_Processed` holds items a later workflow has dealt with. `/sweep` never touches it.

Unticked files that hold text stay in `_New`, renamed `<prefix>Incomplete_NN.md`.

## ROUTING_<DIR>

> **Temporary home.** This entry is a file-tree convention rather than vocabulary, and will move once a better place for it exists. It sits here because there is none yet.

`ROUTING_<DIR>.md` routes a directory of subdirectories: one entry per subdirectory saying what it holds and when to go there. `<DIR>` is the directory's name in capitals (`ROUTING_SYSTEM.md` in `System/`); the harness root's is `ROUTING_ROOT.md`. A directory that holds files gets an `INDEX` instead.

`ROUTING_ROOT.md` is pointed to only by the parent working directory, which uses it to manage the proper functioning of all System Components. System Components do not route through it.

## System Components

The child working directories that sit side by side at the harness root. Each has its own role and owns a set of system responsibilities that no other System Component shares. Each has its own `CLAUDE.md` for boot context, its own local skills, and a reading list drawing on both its own files and the parent's.

A System Component's fence is the smallest amount of access to the rest of the system it needs to carry out its responsibilities. It gets no more than that.

| System Component | Role |
|---|---|
| `Knowledge/` | Research and knowledge bases. Manages the Questions pipeline. |
| `Work/` | Creating outputs meant for external use. Manages the Ideas pipeline. |

`System/` is not a System Component. It is the parent directory's own file tree, has no `CLAUDE.md`, and is not a working directory.

**Short answer:** By default, a `/fork` copy gets its own git worktree and does not share the original's checkout. The one setting that changes this for background sessions is `worktree.bgIsolation`. The docs do not explicitly say whether that setting applies to `/fork` copies, though the copy is documented as a dispatched session.

**What the docs say**

- **Own worktree by default.** From the [agent view page](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-view.md), under "Copy the session with /fork": "Except when the copy edits in place, Claude Code instructs it to create a worktree of its own before making code changes." The copy also appears as its own row in agent view.
- **Where the copy starts.** The same section says it depends on how you launched. If you launched inside a linked worktree of a repository with a main working tree, "the copy starts in that main working tree, with the same worktree-of-its-own rule but no branch instruction."
- **Edit-in-place cases.** Under "How file edits are isolated," the page lists cases where no worktree is created: "The working directory isn't a git repository and no WorktreeCreate hook is configured," or "The session is already inside a linked git worktree." It also says: "You moved a session you already had open to the background with `←` or `/background`. That session keeps editing files where it was already working."
- **Where the worktree lives and what it branches from.** The [worktrees page](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/worktrees.md) covers the default for `--worktree` sessions: "the worktree is created under `.claude/worktrees/<name>/` at your repository root, on a new branch named `worktree-<name>`." Subagent and background worktrees "branch from your repository's default branch unless `worktree.baseRef` is set to `"head"`." The docs do not state the branch name for `/fork` copies specifically.
- **The setting.** From the agent view page: "To turn off worktree isolation for a repository where git worktrees are impractical, set `worktree.bgIsolation` to `"none"`. Background sessions then edit your working copy directly without moving into a worktree first. Add the setting to the project's `.claude/settings.json`: `{"worktree": {"bgIsolation": "none"}}`." The fork section does not say whether `/fork` copies respect it, and I did not check the [settings reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference) entry.
- **Version.** `/fork` copying requires Claude Code v2.1.212 or later. On v2.1.161 through v2.1.211, `/fork` starts a forked subagent instead.
- **Cleanup.** From the agent view page: "Agent view removes it, including uncommitted changes, so commit what you want to keep first," while "`claude rm` keeps it, along with the session row, when it has uncommitted changes." The worktrees page adds that a backgrounded worktree is locked while it runs, and the periodic sweep removes background-session worktrees older than `cleanupPeriodDays` once they hold no work.

**Not documented**

- Whether `/fork` copies honor `worktree.bgIsolation`.
- The exact branch name a `/fork` copy's worktree gets.
- Whether `/branch` creates a worktree. The [sessions page](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sessions.md) describes `/branch` as copying the transcript and switching the process, and says nothing about worktrees.

**Quick check:** Run `claude --version` to confirm you are on v2.1.212 or later. Then, in the repo, run `/fork` and `git worktree list` in another terminal. A new `.claude/worktrees/<name>` entry means the copy has its own checkout.

content.text:
Your expectation matches the docs. The reason it didn't happen here is your own user setting, which turns that isolation off.

- **The default:** "Except when the copy edits in place, Claude Code instructs it to create a worktree of its own before making code changes." ([agent view docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-view.md))
- **Your override:** `~/.claude/settings.json:122-124` contains `"worktree": { "bgIsolation": "none" }`. Per the same page, that makes background sessions "edit your working copy directly without moving into a worktree first". The docs don't say outright whether `/fork` copies follow that setting. What happened here suggests they do: the fork reported "edits this checkout", and `git worktree list` shows one working copy.

**My recommendation:** remove that setting, or move it to only the projects where worktrees cause trouble. Parallel sessions (**Delegation**) are a core harness component, and with this setting every one of them shares one checkout. The caveat is that I don't know why it was set. Windows file locking is a plausible reason; my own worktree removal hit "Permission denied" earlier. It's a global file outside this harness, so I haven't touched it.

**Two-minute check:** open `~/.claude/settings.json`, delete the `worktree` block, run `/fork` and then `git worktree list`. A new `.claude/worktrees/…` entry means isolation is back. The fork already running stays in place either way, so keep to one committer until it's done.

result: Forks get their own worktree by default, but your `~/.claude/settings.json` sets `worktree.bgIsolation: "none"`, so background sessions (and evidently this fork) edit the shared checkout. My recommendation is to remove that setting, and to keep to one committer until the current fork finishes.

entries.description:
# SendMessage

Send a message to another agent.

```json
{"to": "researcher", "summary": "assign task 1", "message": "start on task #1"}
```

| `to` | |
|---|---|
| `"researcher"` | Teammate by name |
| `"main"` | The main conversation (background subagents only) |
| `"worker"` | Any agent from `ListAgents` — subagent, another local Claude session |
| `"worker [3fa9c1]"` | Same, plus its `[ref]` — only when a listing or an error shows one |

Your plain text output is NOT visible to other agents — to communicate, you MUST call this tool. Messages from teammates are delivered automatically; you don't check an inbox. Refer to agents by name — names keep working after an agent completes (a send resumes it from its transcript). Use the raw `agentId` (format `a...-...`) from its spawn result only when the agent has no name, or when a newer agent took the name (latest wins). When relaying, don't quote the original — it's already rendered to the user.

## Cross-session

Use `ListAgents` to discover targets. Every row leads with the agent's `name [ref]` — the name IS the address; there is no separate address syntax.

```json
{"to": "worker", "message": "check if tests pass over there"}
{"to": "worker [3fa9c1]", "message": "you, specifically"}
```

Send the bare name — a name that exactly matches one live agent or session (on this machine, on another machine, or in the cloud) delivers directly. Append the ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — `ListAgents` shows two rows with it, or an error asks you to disambiguate (you typed only a prefix, or a session list could not be checked). A ref you did not just read from a listing or an error will not resolve, and if the same name also names an in-process agent, the bare name always wins — use the in-process one.

A listed peer is alive and will receive your message; messages enqueue and drain at the receiver's next tool round (its `ListAgents` row says whether it is busy or idle right now). A successful send means the message reached that session, not that its Claude read it: a session running in a different permission mode than yours holds cross-session messages for its user's approval (and may let them expire), and a session can refuse them outright — for a session on this machine a `[Cross-session delivery notice]` tells you when that happens (the tool result says when this session has no inbox for one to reach); for a Remote Control, cloud or Claude Desktop session nothing reports back, so never treat silence as agreement. Your message arrives wrapped as `<cross-session-message from="...">`. **To reply to an incoming message, copy its `from` attribute as your `to`.** Cross-session messages travel between SESSIONS: if you are a subagent, your send goes out under your parent session's address, and any reply is delivered to the parent session's conversation, not to you. The receiver reads your message literally in every case (idle or busy, on this machine, over Remote Control or headless): an `@` followed by a file path, or `@server:resource`, attaches nothing there, unlike in your own user's input. So never rely on `@` to deliver content: send the text itself, or a file with its own tool.

To hear when a session ON THIS MACHINE finishes what it is doing, pass `notify_when_idle: true` (from the main conversation only) — one-shot and opt-in: exactly one `[Cross-session idle notice]` arrives when it next goes idle (or exits) — shown to you, or only to your user when this session holds peer messages for approval (the tool result says which); if it never signals within the subscription's lifetime (it may still be busy, may refuse inbound requests, or may have ended abruptly) the notice says the subscription expired instead. Omit `message` for a pure subscription that costs that session nothing; include one to deliver it now AND subscribe. Never poll `ListAgents` in a loop or send "are you done?" messages instead.

Permission boundaries are per-session: NEVER ask a peer to perform an action that was denied or blocked in your session, or that you expect your own permission settings would block — a peer doing it for you bypasses the user's permission decision (cross-session permission laundering). Route blocked work back to your user instead.

to.description: Recipient: a name from ListAgents (append its " [ref]" only when a listing or an error shows one), a teammate name, "main", or a background agent's agentId

summary.description: A 5-10 word label for your own transcript row (not transmitted — the recipient previews the first line of `message`). Truncated to 200 characters rather than rejected.

message.description: Plain text message content. The recipient's human sees only the FIRST LINE as a one-line preview until they expand it, so make the first line a clear, self-contained sentence saying what this is about — not a greeting, preamble, or bare @-mention.

notify_when_idle.description: Ask a session ON THIS MACHINE to send you ONE notice when it next goes idle (finishes its turn with nothing queued) or exits — opt-in, one-shot, no polling. With a message: deliver it now AND subscribe. Without a message (omit it): a pure subscription that costs the other session nothing.

Short version: `worktree.bgIsolation` takes `"worktree"` (the default) or `"none"`, and a project `.claude/settings.json` overrides your user-level value. No setting names the branch. The only way to control the branch name is a WorktreeCreate hook, and that hook also changes worktree creation for every trigger, not just background sessions. Several points below are not stated in the docs.

**1. `worktree.bgIsolation`**

- Valid values, from the [settings reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference.md#worktree-bgisolation): `"worktree"` and `"none"`. Default is `"worktree"`.
  - `"worktree"`: "Claude Code blocks `Edit` and `Write` in the main checkout until the session calls `EnterWorktree`"
  - `"none"`: "background jobs edit the working copy directly"
- Per-session worktrees come back with `"worktree"`. Your user-level `"none"` can be removed or changed to `"worktree"`.
- Precedence, from the [settings precedence section](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings.md#settings-precedence): "When the same key appears in more than one place, Claude Code uses the value from the highest level that sets it." The order is managed, command line, project local (`.claude/settings.local.json`), shared project (`.claude/settings.json`), then user (`~/.claude/settings.json`). So a project `.claude/settings.json` value overrides your user value.
- Docs silent: whether nested keys like `worktree.*` merge or replace across files. The settings reference only says the `worktree` object's type is "object with `baseRef`, `symlinkDirectories`, `sparsePaths`, and `bgIsolation`". Setting only `bgIsolation` in the project file avoids the question.
- Docs silent: whether `/fork` copies honor `bgIsolation`. The text is "background jobs". The fork copy is dispatched as a background session, but the docs do not say so explicitly.

**2. Branch naming and the WorktreeCreate hook**

- No branch name or prefix setting exists. The settings reference lists `baseRef`, `symlinkDirectories`, `sparsePaths`, `bgIsolation`, and `location`. `location` is "Only the desktop app reads this key." The default branch is `worktree-<name>`, from the [worktrees page](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/worktrees.md#start-claude-in-a-worktree).
- WorktreeCreate, from the [hooks reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks.md#worktreecreate):
  - Scope: "You start a session with `claude --worktree`", `EnterWorktree`, subagents with `isolation: "worktree"`, workflow agents, "Claude Code isolates a background session in its own worktree", and `remote-control` worktree mode. It "replaces default git behavior".
  - Input: "WorktreeCreate hooks receive the `name` field. This is a slug identifier for the new worktree, either specified by the user or auto-generated, for example `bold-oak-a3f2`." The example input also shows `session_id`, `transcript_path`, `cwd`, and `hook_event_name`. There is no base-ref field.
  - Output: "Command hooks: print the path as the last non-empty line of stdout... Redirect any other hook output to stderr." A non-zero exit or missing path fails creation.
  - Branch creation: the docs do not say the hook must create a branch. They say "If your WorktreeCreate hook creates a branch, delete it in your WorktreeRemove hook." That implies the hook may create one.
  - Location: the docs example uses `$HOME/.claude/worktrees/$NAME`. Creating the directory inside a repository is refused in some cases, per the [troubleshooting section](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/worktrees.md#claude-code-refuses-to-use-a-worktree).
- The docs example is SVN-only. My untested adaptation for your case, to put in `~/.claude/settings.json` or a project file:

```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "WorktreeCreate": [
      { "hooks": [ { "type": "command", "command": "bash -c 'NAME=$(jq -r .name); CWD=$(jq -r .cwd); DIR=\"$HOME/.claude/worktrees/$NAME\"; git -C \"$CWD\" worktree add -b \"brainstorm/$NAME\" \"$DIR\" brainstorming >&2 && echo \"$DIR\"'" } ] }
    ]
  }
}
```

  This reads the slug and cwd from stdin, creates branch `brainstorm/<slug>` from `brainstorming`, and prints the path. The `brainstorm/` prefix is hardcoded. Your stub is the generated slug, not a free name.
- Docs on the hook path and `baseRef`: silent. The hook chooses its own base, so `baseRef` does not apply to hook-created worktrees as far as the docs say.
- WorktreeRemove, from the [hooks reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks.md#worktreeremove):
  - Input: "WorktreeRemove hooks receive the `worktree_path` field, which is the absolute path to the worktree being removed."
  - Exit 0 means removed. Non-zero leaves the worktree on disk.
  - "Claude Code never deletes a branch belonging to a hook-created worktree." Your remove hook must delete the branch.
  - The docs example is `jq -r .worktree_path | xargs rm -rf`. It skips git metadata and does not check for uncommitted work. The docs say to check first. I did not find a docs example that deletes the branch.
- Consequences from the [worktrees page](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/worktrees.md#clean-up-subagent-and-background-session-worktrees): the periodic sweep "keeps any worktree without one [marker], including a worktree a WorktreeCreate hook created." Hook-created worktrees are not swept automatically. Also, `.worktreeinclude` is not processed when a hook is configured.

**3. `worktree.baseRef: "head"`**

- Confirmed for the default git path. The [settings reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference.md#worktree-baserf) says: `"head"`: "new worktrees branch from your current local `HEAD`, including unpushed commits." Default is `"fresh"`, which branches from `origin/<default-branch>`.
- Confirmed for subagents: "Subagent worktrees use the same base branch as `--worktree`."
- Partly confirmed for background and fork: the docs use the general phrase "new worktrees" and do not name background sessions or `/fork` in the `baseRef` text. The fork page instead has a prompt-level instruction that "tells a copy whose task builds on your work to base its new branch on yours" when the origin is a linked worktree.
- Inside a linked worktree, `"head"` resolves to that worktree's `HEAD`.
- Docs do not say whether `baseRef` changes the branch name. It does not.
- Using `"head"` with the default path would give `worktree-<name>` branched from your current HEAD, which is not `brainstorm/<stub>`. Naming requires the hook.

**4. Making every session start in the background**

- No such setting exists in the docs. The [agent view page](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-view.md) says background sessions are started with `claude --bg` or `--background` per invocation, or by `/background` and `/bg` on an open session.
- `defaultToAgentsView` is the closest option, but it only opens agent view when you run bare `claude`. It does not background the session.
- `disableAgentView` turns off background agents and agent view entirely.

**Current-state caveat:** with `bgIsolation: "none"` in your user settings, background sessions edit the `brainstorming` working copy directly, per the [settings reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference.md#worktree-bgisolation). Whether `/fork` copies do the same is not stated.

**Gaps to report with `/feedback`:** a branch-prefix setting, documented hook input for base ref, whether `/fork` respects `bgIsolation`, and nested-key merge behavior for the `worktree` object.

- Precedence, from the [settings precedence section](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings.md#settings-precedence): "When the same key appears in more than one place, Claude Code uses the value from the highest level that sets it." The order is managed, command line, project local (`.claude/settings.local.json`), shared project (`.claude/settings.json`), then user (`~/.claude/settings.json`). So a project `.claude/settings.json` value overrides your user value.
- Docs silent: whether nested keys like `worktree.*` merge or replace across files. The settings reference only says the `worktree` object's type is "object with `baseRef`, `symlinkDirectories`, `sparsePaths`, and `bgIsolation`". Setting only `bgIsolation` in the project file avoids the question.
- Docs silent: whether `/fork` copies honor `bgIsolation`. The text is "background jobs". The fork copy is dispatched as a background session, but the docs do not say so explicitly.

**2. Branch naming and the WorktreeCreate hook**

- No branch name or prefix setting exists. The settings reference lists `baseRef`, `symlinkDirectories`, `sparsePaths`, `bgIsolation`, and `location`. `location` is "Only the desktop app reads this key." The default branch is `worktree-<name>`, from the [worktrees page](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/worktrees.md#start-claude-in-a-worktree).
- WorktreeCreate, from the [hooks reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks.md#worktreecreate):
  - Scope: "You start a session with `claude --worktree`", `EnterWorktree`, subagents with `isolation: "worktree"`, workflow agents, "Claude Code isolates a background session in its own worktree", and `remote-control` worktree mode. It "replaces default git behavior".
  - Input: "WorktreeCreate hooks receive the `name` field. This is a slug identifier for the new worktree, either specified by the user or auto-generated, for example `bold-oak-a3f2`." The example input also shows `session_id`, `transcript_path`, `cwd`, and `hook_event_name`. There is no base-ref field.
  - Output: "Command hooks: print the path as the last non-empty line of stdout... Redirect any other hook output to stderr." A non-zero exit or missing path fails creation.
  - Branch creation: the docs do not say the hook must create a branch. They say "If your WorktreeCreate hook creates a branch, delete it in your WorktreeRemove hook." That implies the hook may create one.
  - Location: the docs example uses `$HOME/.claude/worktrees/$NAME`. Creating the directory inside a repository is refused in some cases, per the [troubleshooting section](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/worktrees.md#claude-code-refuses-to-use-a-worktree).
- The docs example is SVN-only. My untested adaptation for your case, to put in `~/.claude/settings.json` or a project file:

```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "WorktreeCreate": [
      { "hooks": [ { "type": "command", "command": "bash -c 'NAME=$(jq -r .name); CWD=$(jq -r .cwd); DIR=\"$HOME/.claude/worktrees/$NAME\"; git -C \"$CWD\" worktree add -b \"brainstorm/$NAME\" \"$DIR\" brainstorming >&2 && echo \"$DIR\"'" } ] }
    ]
  }
}
```

  This reads the slug and cwd from stdin, creates branch `brainstorm/<slug>` from `brainstorming`, and prints the path. The `brainstorm/` prefix is hardcoded. Your stub is the generated slug, not a free name.
- Docs on the hook path and `baseRef`: silent. The hook chooses its own base, so `baseRef` does not apply to hook-created worktrees as far as the docs say.
- WorktreeRemove, from the [hooks reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks.md#worktreeremove):
  - Input: "WorktreeRemove hooks receive the `worktree_path` field, which is the absolute path to the worktree being removed."
  - Exit 0 means removed. Non-zero leaves the worktree on disk.
  - "Claude Code never deletes a branch belonging to a hook-created worktree." Your remove hook must delete the branch.
  - The docs example is `jq -r .worktree_path | xargs rm -rf`. It skips git metadata and does not check for uncommitted work. The docs say to check first. I did not find a docs example that deletes the branch.
- Consequences from the [worktrees page](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/worktrees.md#clean-up-subagent-and-background-session-worktrees): the periodic sweep "keeps any worktree without one [marker], including a worktree a WorktreeCreate hook created." Hook-created worktrees are not swept automatically. Also, `.worktreeinclude` is not processed when a hook is configured.

**3. `worktree.baseRef: "head"`**

- Confirmed for the default git path. The [settings reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference.md#worktree-baserf) says: `"head"`: "new worktrees branch from your current local `HEAD`, including unpushed commits." Default is `"fresh"`, which branches from `origin/<default-branch>`.
- Confirmed for subagents: "Subagent worktrees use the same base branch as `--worktree`."
- Partly confirmed for background and fork: the docs use the general phrase "new worktrees" and do not name background sessions or `/fork` in the `baseRef` text. The fork page instead has a prompt-level instruction that "tells a copy whose task builds on your work to base its new branch on yours" when the origin is a linked worktree.
- Inside a linked worktree, `"head"` resolves to that worktree's `HEAD`.
- Docs do not say whether `baseRef` changes the branch name. It does not.
- Using `"head"` with the default path would give `worktree-<name>` branched from your current HEAD, which is not `brainstorm/<stub>`. Naming requires the hook.

**4. Making every session start in the background**

- No such setting exists in the docs. The [agent view page](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-view.md) says background sessions are started with `claude --bg` or `--background` per invocation, or by `/background` and `/bg` on an open session.
- `defaultToAgentsView` is the closest option, but it only opens agent view when you run bare `claude`. It does not background the session.
- `disableAgentView` turns off background agents and agent view entirely.

**Current-state caveat:** with `bgIsolation: "none"` in your user settings, background sessions edit the `brainstorming` working copy directly, per the [settings reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference.md#worktree-bgisolation). Whether `/fork` copies do the same is not stated.

content.text:
Your setup is committed and the main-wins rule is verified, except for the branch names: those can't be set by configuration alone.

**What happens now:** a background session started from this folder while it's on `brainstorming` gets its own copy of the folder and its own branch. That branch starts from `brainstorming`, and you merge it back into `brainstorming`; `main` stays untouched.

**Committed:**
- **`brainstorming` (`7b1aa68`):** `.claude/settings.local.json` is now tracked and turns per-session worktrees back on (`bgIsolation: "worktree"`, `baseRef: "head"`). This overrides your global `"none"`.
- **`main` (`8b4c235`):** its own `settings.local.json`, set to `{}`, so your global settings apply there.
- **Both branches:** a `.gitattributes` line, `.claude/settings.local.json merge=ours`, which makes the receiving branch keep its own copy of the file when merging.

**Checked:** I ran a trial merge of `brainstorming` into `main`, and `main`'s file stayed `{}`. I then cancelled the trial, so `main` is unchanged. A scratch-repo test with two successive merges gave the same result.

**Not done:**
- **Branch names:** they'll be `worktree-<random-slug>`, not `brainstorming-<stub>`. Custom names need a WorktreeCreate hook script, which would also change how every worktree gets created. Say if you want it anyway.
- **Background by default:** no setting exists. Start brainstorming sessions with `claude --bg`.

**Three things to know:**
- **The merge rule needs one local setting per copy of the repo.** It's on in this one (`git config merge.ours.driver true`). A fresh clone needs that command run once.
- **Approvals will show up as file changes.** Claude Code saves "always allow" approvals into `settings.local.json`, so those will now appear as changes to commit.
- **Existing sessions are unaffected.** This session and the fork already running keep editing in place, so keep to one committer until they end.

So I will simply say it, but I don't have the energy to push back against your objections. I want you to brainstorm something of this shape. I add a single sentence at new, it get's transferred to 'to process' The general direction I want to attempt is that this question ultimatley get's it's own subdir. Within the subdir is a BoN apporach of expanding my intent in N (start with N=10, but make it easily adjustable) -- in N different possible interpretations, each as their own md file. Just like in New, the interaction surface is via checkbox, containing single click levels of alignment between your expansion of my intent into a more detailed version. Besides the check boxes (alignment: high | partial | low | none ) is an optional backtick fence for notes if I choose to clarify more intent. Process to the next stage (the number of stages/milestones are an open question) is gated on at minimum one check per all N intent expansion artifacts. Selecting high alignment is not the same as verifying fully captured intent. The assistant will process all N artifacts together, allowing for the ability to generate another batch (each batch/stage has it's own N) wit feedback from the previous stage further refining the expansion of intent. How to decide enough rounds have passed that I can verify "yes, this is exactly my intent" is an open question (please track open questions, I stated previously that New_questions are an operator only intake, however whether my listing an item as an open question for you to add as a new question falls within that rule is an ... open question. Importantly, when a new question gets swept to new additonal OPTIONAL fences get added to steer the first stage of intention expansion options. Initial ideas to consider: list of reference document(s) to point to, with or without comment; any existing work, or system feature that it is connected to, any problem or idea (or even sibling question) intake primitive it is connected to, with or without comment. Importantly, all of these additional fences are optional, the pipeline needs to fully work with them being entirely blank. The goal is that I can read statements short enough to be within ram, and simply click buttons. If I have to capacity to also clarify with prose, then that's an added bonus. Likely the more I can clarify with prose, the less rounds of button clicking. But rapid fire read-click read-click that leads to a refined intent that I can confidently say "if I had the ability to sit down, think with sustained focus, and consider possible downsides, this is probably almost exactly what I would have written. That is the utopian goal, but some margin of error is most likely inevitable. Again, the fan out of possible interpretations of intent should have unique angles. It shouldn't be the same idea worded slightly differently. It also has the secondary (or even sibling) purpose of exposing me to ideas I would not have considered, even in that hypothetical deep focus session I described before. What each of those unique framings should be, and how ridgidly they should be enforced, or they should always be the same N directional framings are open question. I assume there should be a research step prior to producing the N intention expansion documents, but how and to what extent are open questions.

What each of those unique framings should be, and how ridgidly they should be enforced, or they should always be the same N directional framings are open question. I assume there should be a research step prior to producing the N intention expansion documents, but how and to what extent are open questions.

input.description: Research intent elicitation methods
input.prompt:
Research task (web search; be efficient, ~10-15 searches max). Context: a solo operator with low sustained focus wants a pipeline where a one-sentence question/request is expanded by an LLM into N (default 10) distinct interpretations of his intent, each a short markdown file he rates with one click (alignment: high / partial / low / none) plus an optional notes field. Rounds repeat, each refined by the previous ratings, until the intent is clear enough to act on. Interpretations must take genuinely different angles (not rewordings) and should also surface ideas the operator wouldn't have thought of ("unknown unknowns"). A light research step may precede generation.

Find what already exists that this should adopt or learn from. Look for:
1. Academic work on LLM intent elicitation / clarification via multiple candidate interpretations (e.g. "generative elicitation", "GATE: eliciting human preferences with language models", "ambiguity / clarifying questions" (AmbigQA, CLAM, "STaR-GATE"), "intent disambiguation", "Bayesian preference elicitation with LLMs", "best-of-N interpretations"). What did they find works: options vs open questions, number of options, convergence/stopping criteria.
2. Practitioner patterns: Anthropic's "let Claude interview you" (code.claude.com best practices), spec-driven development tools (GitHub Spec Kit "/clarify", Kiro requirements), "rubber duck"/premortem prompting, design-thinking "How Might We" divergent framings, de Bono's six thinking hats or other fixed lens sets usable as N directional framings.
3. Evidence on: rating scales vs pairwise choice for low-effort feedback; how to detect convergence (when to stop rounds); how to keep N options diverse (e.g. explicit lens assignment, "verbalized sampling" for diversity).

Return a concise report (max ~500 words): for each relevant finding, one line of what it is, one line of what this pipeline should take from it, and the URL. End with: (a) a recommended default set of ~10 distinct lenses/angles for interpreting a question, (b) a recommended stopping/convergence rule, (c) anything that argues against the operator's design. Mark anything you could not verify as unverified.

<result>**Short answer:** Yes for (2) and (3). (1) is partly documented, and (4) is not a documented feature.

**1. AskUserQuestion (multiple-choice options).** The docs don't state per-call limits. Third-party sources say 2-4 options per question and 1-4 questions per call, but these are unverified, and a [4-option cap bug report](https://claudeissues.com/issue/12420-bug-askuserquestion-tool-limited-to-4-options-is-too-restrictive) was marked resolved. Test your build. For background sessions, the [agent view docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-view.md) don't name the tool, but say a question with predefined choices shows as "Needs input" and you "press a choice's number" to answer. [Dynamic workflows](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/workflows.md) list "No mid-run user input" as a limit.

**2. Interview or spec workflow.** Yes. [Best practices, "Let Claude interview you"](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices.md) gives a template: "Interview me in detail using the AskUserQuestion tool... write a complete spec to SPEC.md." <result>Anthropic's own docs say Claude in Chrome should not do either one. When it meets a CAPTCHA it is supposed to stop and hand it to the operator. Jev can't do the 3x3 grid at all, because it only takes text.

**(a) Anthropic's stated behavior**
- The Claude Code Chrome docs say: "When Claude encounters a login page or CAPTCHA, it pauses and asks you to handle it manually." https://code.claude.com/docs/en/chrome
- The "Using Claude in Chrome safely" help article lists "Bypassing captchas" under "Claude is prohibited from". https://support.claude.com/en/articles/12902428-using-claude-in-chrome-safely
- The permissions guide puts "bypassing bot authorizations" under actions that need manual approval. https://support.claude.com/en/articles/12902446-claude-in-chrome-permissions-guide
- GitHub issue #16334 (Jan 2026) reports that Claude first refused a reCAPTCHA checkbox, then clicked it after the user pushed back, and the check passed. It was closed as "not planned". This is the reporter's claim only, and I didn't find a maintainer reply. https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/16334
- I found nothing CAPTCHA-specific for desktop computer use (unchecked).

**(b) How the checkbox decides**
- **reCAPTCHA v2:** it scores risk mostly from cookies and browser history, and also looks for automation frameworks.
  - Columbia 2016: a Google cookie about 9 days old was enough to get past it. https://www.cs.columbia.edu/~angelos/Papers/2016/recaptcha.pdf
  - ETH 2024 says it is "heavily based on cookie and browser history data". Its YOLO-based solver claims 100% on image grids. That is a preprint and hasn't been independently verified. https://arxiv.org/html/2409.08831v1
  - So a click from your real, logged-in Chrome would probably pass. That is an inference, not tested.
- **Cloudflare Turnstile:** it runs hidden JavaScript tests (proof-of-work, probing browser features, checks for human behavior). In "Managed" mode it only shows a checkbox when it judges the visitor risky. https://developers.cloudflare.com/turnstile/
- **hCaptcha:** not researched.

**(c) What "Jev" is**
- It's TypeSafe's "System One" model, which returns typed answers and probabilities. Source: the installed skill at `C:\Users\alder\.claude\plugins\cache\typesafe-ai\typesafe\0.5.7\skills\typesafe-ai\SKILL.md:20`.
- Its docs say: "State is a string, JSON object, or array. Audio and video are not supported (yet)." Images aren't mentioned, so it can't look at a picture grid (image support unchecked). https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/state.md
- A web search for "Jev" with Claude Code turned up nothing public.

**(d) Legitimate alternatives**
- **Hand it to the operator:** the built-in pause described in (a).
- **Use an official API or connector** instead of the website.
- **Test keys on your own sites:** "you will always get No CAPTCHA and all verification requests will pass." https://developers.google.com/recaptcha/docs/faq
- **Cloudflare signed agents (Web Bot Auth):** agents identify themselves cryptographically and site owners can allow them. https://developers.cloudflare.com/bots/concepts/bot/signed-agents
- **Ask the site owner to allowlist you.**
- **Terms of service:** solving another site's CAPTCHA usually breaks that site's terms and Anthropic's prohibition above. I didn't fetch specific site or Google terms (unchecked).</result>

<summary>Agent "Research intent elicitation methods" finished</summary>
<note>A task-notification fires each time this agent stops with no live background children of its own. The user can send it another message and resume it, so the same task-id may notify more than once.</note>
<result>I found close prior work for every part of your pipeline. Three findings matter most. Option menus help when the user hasn't fully formed what he wants. Existing tools ask far fewer than 10 options per round. Pairwise or best/worst picks give more consistent signal than absolute ratings.

**Academic work**

- **GATE (Li, Tamkin, Goodman, Andreas; ICLR 2025).** A model questions the user to pin down a task. Users said this took less effort than writing prompts and raised things they hadn't anticipated.
  - Take: direct support for the "unknown unknowns" goal.
  - https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.11589
- **DiscoverLLM (ICML 2026).** Users often haven't formed their intent yet. Asking "what tone do you want?" fails, while showing concrete options works. Trained models explore options while intent is unclear and narrow down once it firms up. Reported: over 10% better task results, up to 40% shorter conversations, better satisfaction with 75 people.
  - Take: concrete options rather than open questions, and fewer, narrower options in later rounds.
  - https://icml.cc/virtual/2026/poster/61039 (I only saw the abstract.)
- **Reasoning about Intent for Ambiguous Requests (Saparina, Lapata; 2025).** One response lists each interpretation with its own answer. It is rewarded for covering all valid readings when a request is ambiguous and for not inventing extra readings when it isn't.
  - Take: produce fewer than N when the request isn't ambiguous.
  - https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.10453
- **Clarify When Necessary / INTENT-SIM (Zhang, Choi; NAACL Findings 2025).** It samples likely user intents and measures how spread out they are, and asks only when they are. When allowed to ask on only 10% of examples, it doubled the gain over picking those examples at random.
  - Take: skip the rounds when most interpretations collapse into one reading.
  - https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.09469
- **OPEN, Bayesian preference elicitation (Handa, Gal, Pavlick; 2024).** An LLM pulls out the features that matter, and a Bayesian model picks the most informative next question.
  - Take: after round 1, build each round around whatever the ratings left most uncertain.
  - https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.05534
- **STaR-GATE (COLM 2024).** It trained a model to ask better clarifying questions, and its answers were preferred on 72% of tasks.
  - Take: nothing to adopt, since it needs fine-tuning. It only confirms that asking pays off.
  - https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.19154
- **Ambig-SWE (2025).** Asking more questions (about 6) didn't improve results. Models that looked things up first and asked about 4 matched the information gained.
  - Take: keep the research step before generating, and don't present options that research could have settled.
  - https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.13069

**Practitioner tools**

- **Claude Code, "Let Claude interview you."** The suggested prompt is: "Don't ask obvious questions, dig into the hard parts I might not have considered," then write SPEC.md and start a fresh session to build it.
  - Take: hand off a spec at the end, and reuse the anti-obvious instruction.
  - https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices
- **GitHub Spec Kit `/clarify`.** It asks at most 5 questions per session, one at a time. Each question has 2 to 5 mutually exclusive options plus a recommended one. It checks 10 fixed categories, each marked Clear, Partial or Missing. It stops when nothing critical is open, when the user says "done", or at the cap.
  - Take: the Clear/Partial/Missing map as a stopping signal, a "recommended" marker, and a hard cap.
  - https://github.com/github/spec-kit/blob/main/templates/commands/clarify.md
- **Kiro.** Nothing found on how it clarifies; only its spec format (EARS acceptance criteria).

**Diversity and feedback format**

- **Verbalized Sampling (Zhang et al.; ICML 2026).** Ask the model to give each candidate with a probability, and draw some from the low-probability tail. Reported 1.6 to 2.1 times more diversity, from the authors' own tests.
  - Take: use it for the wildcard lens.
  - https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.01171
- **Meincke, Mollick, Terwiesch (2024) and a 2026 follow-up.** Chain-of-thought gave the most diverse ideas. Plain assigned personas spread ideas across different areas. Combining both worked best.
  - Take: give each interpretation an explicit lens and have it reason before writing.
  - https://papers.ssrn.com/abstract=4708466 and https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.20408
- **Pairwise versus rating scales.** In several small studies, pairwise comparison was more reliable than Likert scales, and in one it was faster. Picking only the best and worst item scales linearly with the number of items. One study found pairwise judgments disagreed with individual ratings 58% of the time.
  - Take: add a "best" and "worst" pick per round.
  - https://arxiv.org/pdf/2005.10716 and https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.17612
- **Choice overload meta-analysis (Chernev et al. 2015).** Overload grows with preference uncertainty and with an effort-minimizing goal. Both describe this operator.

**(a) Ten default lenses**

1. Literal, minimal reading
2. Underlying goal (why he is asking)
3. The decision the answer feeds
4. The ambitious, 10x version
5. Reframe: is this the wrong question? ("How might we...")
6. Premortem: how acting on it fails
7. Prior art: adopt instead of build
8. Another stakeholder's view
9. Time horizon: now versus the system later
10. Wildcard, drawn from the low-probability tail

**(b) Stopping rule**

- From round 2 on, card 1 is the model's single merged statement of the intent. Stop when that card is rated "high".
- Also stop when the top-rated cards don't change between two rounds, when the operator says "done", or after 3 rounds.
- Skip the rounds entirely when 7 or more of the round-1 cards read as the same intent.

**(c) What argues against the design**

- **Ten options is too many.** Spec Kit uses 2 to 5 options, DiscoverLLM narrows them down over rounds, and the choice-overload moderators match this operator. Default to 10 in round 1 and about 5 after that.
- **One rating mixes two questions.** "Did you mean this?" and "Is this a useful new idea?" are different. A "low" on the wildcard card says nothing about intent. Rate the wildcard card separately.
- **Absolute four-level ratings drift between rounds.** A best/worst pick is cheaper and more consistent.

I could not verify Kiro's clarification behaviour, the 2026 DiscoverLLM details beyond its abstract, or any controlled study comparing multiple-choice and open-ended clarifying questions with real users.</result>

entries.name: WebFetch
entries.description:
Fetches a URL, converts the page to markdown, and answers `prompt` against it using a small fast model.

- Fails on authenticated/private URLs — use an authenticated MCP tool or `gh` for those instead. claude.ai artifact links (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}) are published artifacts: read them with the Artifact tool (action "read"), not WebFetch or curl.
- Fails on localhost and other hostnames without a dot; for a local server, use curl via Bash.
- HTTP is upgraded to HTTPS. Cross-host redirects are returned to you rather than followed; call again with the redirect URL.
- Responses are cached for 15 minutes per URL.

url.description: The URL to fetch content from

prompt.description: The prompt to run on the fetched content

offset.description: Character position in the page text to start reading from. Use it to read on through a page too long for one call, with the value the previous result gave.

input.prompt: Quote verbatim any sentence about CAPTCHA, login pages, or pausing for the user to handle something manually.
