# Pipeline contract (shared by every draft pipeline)

Written by the assistant on 2026-10-15 for the overnight experiment on a brainstorming branch. Every pipeline turns one operator sentence (a question or idea) into a confirmed statement of intent at the level of detail of the operator's snippets in `System/Snippets/`.

## Run folder

Each run works only inside its own run folder:

- `QUESTION.md`: the operator's sentence (never edited)
- `CONTEXT.md`: optional operator fences (blank in the experiment)
- `Round_01/`, `Round_02/`, ...: one folder per round of operator interaction
  - `ROUND.md`: assistant notes for the round; the operator never needs to read it
  - interaction files: what the operator reads and ticks
- `INTENT.md`: the final artifact, written when the pipeline stops expanding

## Interaction files

- A tick is `- [x]`. An unticked box is `- [ ]`. The operator ticks; the assistant never does.
- Free text goes only in fenced blocks named `notes`, which the operator may leave blank.
- Every file the operator must read states at the top how many boxes need a tick.
- Keep each file within Operator RAM: one idea per file where possible, short sentences, plain words.
- In the experiment, a simulated operator does the ticking and appends a line to `Round_NN/SIMULATED.md`. Simulated input is never presented as the operator's.

## INTENT.md (same for every pipeline)

Sections, in this order:

1. `# Intent: <the operator's sentence>`
2. `## In the operator's voice (draft by the assistant)`: 120-300 words, first person, plain and direct like the operator's snippets: what he wants, why, what it feeds, what he rules out, what would make the answer useless.
3. `## Structured`: bullets for Goal; Why / decision it feeds; Constraints; Ruled out; What a good answer must contain; Unknown unknowns worth keeping; Still open.
4. `## Confirm`: three checkboxes, `- [ ] Yes, this is my intent`, `- [ ] Close (say what is off in the notes)`, `- [ ] No`, then an empty fenced block named `notes`.

"Yes" confirms. "Close" or "No" sends the pipeline back for one more round (unless the round cap is reached), and the notes are the main input to that round.

## Hard rules

- Never answer the question; only clarify the intent behind it.
- Never invent commitments the operator did not express or confirm; mark guesses as guesses (under "Still open").
- Read only: the run folder, the shared research brief named in the prompt, `System/Snippets/` (to learn the operator's voice), the pipeline protocol, and harness files the question points to.

entries.name: CronCreate
entries.description:
Schedule a prompt to be enqueued at a future time. Use for both recurring schedules and one-shot reminders.

Uses standard 5-field cron in the user's local timezone: minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week. "0 9 * * *" means 9am local — no timezone conversion needed.

## One-shot tasks (recurring: false)

For "remind me at X" or "at <time>, do Y" requests — fire once then auto-delete.
Pin minute/hour/day-of-month/month to specific values:
  "remind me at 2:30pm today to check the deploy" → cron: "30 14 <today_dom> <today_month> *", recurring: false
  "tomorrow morning, run the smoke test" → cron: "57 8 <tomorrow_dom> <tomorrow_month> *", recurring: false

## Recurring jobs (recurring: true, the default)

For "every N minutes" / "every hour" / "weekdays at 9am" requests:
  "*/5 * * * *" (every 5 min), "0 * * * *" (hourly), "0 9 * * 1-5" (weekdays at 9am local)

## Avoid the :00 and :30 minute marks when the task allows it

Every user who asks for "9am" gets `0 9`, and every user who asks for "hourly" gets `0 *` — which means requests from across the planet land on the API at the same instant. When the user's request is approximate, pick a minute that is NOT 0 or 30:
  "every morning around 9" → "57 8 * * *" or "3 9 * * *" (not "0 9 * * *")
  "hourly" → "7 * * * *" (not "0 * * * *")
  "in an hour or so, remind me to..." → pick whatever minute you land on, don't round

Only use minute 0 or 30 when the user names that exact time and clearly means it ("at 9:00 sharp", "at half past", coordinating with a meeting). When in doubt, nudge a few minutes early or late — the user will not notice, and the fleet will.

## Session-only

Jobs live only in this Claude session — nothing is written to disk, and the job is gone when Claude exits.

## Not for live watching

CronCreate re-runs a prompt at fixed wall-clock intervals. To watch a log file, process, or command output and be notified the moment something changes, use the Monitor tool instead — Monitor streams events as they happen; cron polls on a schedule.

## Runtime behavior

Jobs only fire while the REPL is idle (not mid-query). The scheduler shifts each job by a fixed per-job offset on top of whatever you pick: by default a recurring job runs up to 50% of its period late (max 30 min), and a one-shot job landing on :00 or :30 runs up to 90 s early. The result of this tool and of CronList gives each job's actual next run time: when you tell the user when a job will run, give that time, not the minute in the cron expression. Picking an off-minute is still the bigger lever.

Recurring tasks auto-expire after 7 days — they fire one final time, then are deleted. This bounds session lifetime. Tell the user about the 7-day limit when scheduling recurring jobs.

Returns a job ID you can pass to CronDelete.

cron.description: Standard 5-field cron expression in local time: "M H DoM Mon DoW" (e.g. "*/5 * * * *" = every 5 minutes, "30 14 28 2 *" = Feb 28 at 2:30pm local once).

prompt.description: The prompt to enqueue at each fire time.

recurring.description: true (default) = fire on every cron match until deleted or auto-expired after 7 days. false = fire once at the next match, then auto-delete. Use false for "remind me at X" one-shot requests with pinned minute/hour/dom/month.

durable.description: Has no effect — durable persistence is not available. All jobs are session-only (in-memory, gone when this Claude session ends).

entries.name: TaskCreate
entries.description:
Use this tool to create a structured task list for your current coding session. This helps you track progress, organize complex tasks, and demonstrate thoroughness to the user.
It also helps the user understand the progress of the task and overall progress of their requests.

## When to Use This Tool

Use this tool proactively in these scenarios:

- Complex multi-step tasks - When a task requires 3 or more distinct steps or actions
- Non-trivial and complex tasks - Tasks that require careful planning or multiple operations
- Plan mode - When using plan mode, create a task list to track the work
- User explicitly requests todo list - When the user directly asks you to use the todo list
- User provides multiple tasks - When users provide a list of things to be done (numbered or comma-separated)
- After receiving new instructions - Immediately capture user requirements as tasks
- When you start working on a task - Mark it as in_progress BEFORE beginning work
- After completing a task - Mark it as completed and add any new follow-up tasks discovered during implementation

## When NOT to Use This Tool

Skip using this tool when:
- There is only a single, straightforward task
- The task is trivial and tracking it provides no organizational benefit
- The task can be completed in less than 3 trivial steps
- The task is purely conversational or informational

NOTE that you should not use this tool if there is only one trivial task to do. In this case you are better off just doing the task directly.

## Task Fields

- **subject**: A brief, actionable title in imperative form (e.g., "Fix authentication bug in login flow")
- **description**: What needs to be done
- **activeForm** (optional): Present continuous form shown in the spinner when the task is in_progress (e.g., "Fixing authentication bug"). If omitted, the spinner shows the subject instead.

All tasks are created with status `pending`.

## Tips

- Create tasks with clear, specific subjects that describe the outcome
- After creating tasks, use TaskUpdate to set up dependencies (blocks/blockedBy) if needed
- Check TaskList first to avoid creating duplicate tasks

subject.description: A brief title for the task

activeForm.description: Present continuous form shown in spinner when in_progress (e.g., "Running tests")

metadata.description: Arbitrary metadata to attach to the task

entries.name: TaskUpdate
entries.description:
Use this tool to update a task in the task list.

## When to Use This Tool

**Mark tasks as resolved:**
- When you have completed the work described in a task
- When a task is no longer needed or has been superseded
- IMPORTANT: Always mark your assigned tasks as resolved when you finish them
- After resolving, call TaskList to find your next task

- ONLY mark a task as completed when you have FULLY accomplished it
- If you encounter errors, blockers, or cannot finish, keep the task as in_progress
- When blocked, create a new task describing what needs to be resolved
- Never mark a task as completed if:
  - Tests are failing
  - Implementation is partial
  - You encountered unresolved errors
  - You couldn't find necessary files or dependencies

**Delete tasks:**
- When a task is no longer relevant or was created in error
- Setting status to `deleted` permanently removes the task

**Update task details:**
- When requirements change or become clearer
- When establishing dependencies between tasks

## Fields You Can Update

- **status**: The task status (see Status Workflow below)
- **subject**: Change the task title (imperative form, e.g., "Run tests")
- **description**: Change the task description
- **activeForm**: Present continuous form shown in spinner when in_progress (e.g., "Running tests")
- **owner**: Change the task owner (agent name)
- **metadata**: Merge metadata keys into the task (set a key to null to delete it)
- **addBlocks**: Mark tasks that cannot start until this one completes
- **addBlockedBy**: Mark tasks that must complete before this one can start

## Status Workflow

Status progresses: `pending` → `in_progress` → `completed`

Use `deleted` to permanently remove a task.

## Staleness

Make sure to read a task's latest state using `TaskGet` before updating it.

## Examples

Mark task as in progress when starting work:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "status": "in_progress"}
```

Mark task as completed after finishing work:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "status": "completed"}
```

Delete a task:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "status": "deleted"}
```

Claim a task by setting owner:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "owner": "my-name"}
```

Set up task dependencies:
```json
{"taskId": "2", "addBlockedBy": ["1"]}
```

taskId.description: The ID of the task to update

activeForm.description: Present continuous form shown in spinner when in_progress (e.g., "Running tests")

addBlocks.description: Task IDs that this task blocks

addBlockedBy.description: Task IDs that block this task

metadata.description: Metadata keys to merge into the task. Set a key to null to delete it.

content.text:
Here's the plan, already in place, so it doesn't depend on you managing anything:

1. **All the state lives in one committed file, not in my context.** That's `HANDOVER.md` (commit `6efbc15`). It holds the ask (pointers to your three snippets), the paths, the model choices, the pitfalls hit so far, a step checklist and a log. Every step ends with tick, log line, commit. Any session can pick up from the first unchecked step, so sessions don't depend on each other.
2. **My context stays small.** The heavy work runs inside workflows, and only short summaries come back to me. Scores and costs are computed by scripts, not by me reading files. When my context fills, Claude Code compresses it automatically, and the next step starts by re-reading the handover.
3. **An hourly heartbeat keeps it moving** (job `0954c7d1`, every hour at :17). When I'm idle it either carries on with the next step, or simply retries if the last attempt hit a usage limit. That's the one-hour wait-and-retry loop you asked for. It deletes itself when the checklist is done, and expires after 7 days in any case.
4. **The one gap:** the heartbeat lives inside this Claude process. If the machine restarts or the process dies, it's gone, and the only fix is to start a new session yourself with this single line:
   `claude --bg "Read System/Brainstorms/Experiments/2026-10-15/HANDOVER.md in the brainstorming-intent-pipelines worktree and continue"`

**How to check in under two minutes:** open `HANDOVER.md` in the worktree folder `.claude/worktrees/brainstorming-intent-pipelines/`. The checklist shows exactly where things stand.

content.content:
1 --- 2 description: 3 version: 0.1 4 disable-model-invocation: true 5 --- 6 7 # Hot Start 8 9 Spin up your live working set in one shot. For every sprint marked **hot**, open a **normal 10 interactive Claude Code session** in its own Windows Terminal tab — each express-resumed straight 11 onto that sprint's cursor. It's the *attended, right-now* sibling of the overnight 12 `Agentic Orchestration` spawner: same `wt.exe` tab-loop, but the variables are fixed (start = now, 30s 13 stagger, N = how many are hot) and the sessions are yours to drive, not unattended workers. These are 14 **interactive sessions, never headless** — no `-p`/`--print`. 15 16 There is **no board file.** The hot set lives in two frontmatter keys on each sprint's `_SPEC_`, so 17 the launch set is *derived on read* — glob the truthy ones and fire. Nothing to maintain, nothing to 18 clobber, and a finished sprint takes its hot-flag into the archive with it. 19 20 ## Source of truth — two `_SPEC_` frontmatter keys 21 22 Set on each `Projects/

/Sprints//_SPEC_.md`: 23 24 - **`HOT?`** — `Yes` | `No`. `Yes` = part of your live set; absent or `No` = not hot. (YAML parses 25 `Yes`/`No` as booleans, so the launch glob just filters on truthiness.) 26 - **`Color`** — a hex tab color, e.g. `#009999` (short `#099` also valid). **Windows Terminal 27 `--tabColor` accepts hex only** — so the stored value is always hex, **quoted** in YAML 28 (`Color: '#009999'`; an unquoted `#…` is a comment and parses to null); `set` converts a 29 natural-language color to hex before writing. **Missing/blank is normalized to the default `#000000`** 30 (see *Default color* below), so the launch command always carries a `--tabColor`. 31 32 The **tab title is always the sprint name** — no display override. New specs are born with `HOT?: No` 33 and `Color: #000000` from the template; absence of `HOT?` (or `No`) is the off state. 34 35 **Liveness is by location:** only specs that are direct children of `Sprints/` count. The glob is 36 single-level (`Sprints/*/`), so `_Archived Sprints/` is excluded and finished sprints can't resurface. 37 38 ### Default color — `#000000` 39 40 Every tab gets a `--tabColor`, so the launch command is always the same shape. A spec with no color 41 isn't left blank — it's normalized to **`#000000`** (black). Black is deliberate: it blends with 42 Windows Terminal's dark tab bar, so a *default* tab reads as uncolored, while the ones you actually 43 color stand out. 44 45 **Normalization writes back — but never bumps `updated`.** Whenever the skill reads a live spec (in 46 `set` or at launch) and finds `Color` missing or blank, it writes `Color: #000000` into that spec's 47 frontmatter, leaving `updated` (and `updated_by`, if present) **untouched**. The write makes the spec 48 explicit and the command uniform; preserving `updated` keeps an auto-default from polluting the 49 recency sort — a spec touched only by normalization shouldn't jump to "most recently updated." The 50 default value lives only here in the skill: that's its single source of truth (the spec template seeds 51 the same literal for new sprints). 52 53 ## `/hot-start` (no argument) — launch 54 55 1. Glob `Projects/*/Sprints/*/_SPEC_*.md` (single-level — **never** `**`). Read each spec's 56 frontmatter: `project`, `sprint`, `HOT?`, `Color` (normalize a missing/blank `Color` to `#000000`, 57 no `updated` bump). 58 2. Keep the rows where `HOT?` is truthy. 59 3. **No hot specs → fall into `set`** (below). There's nothing to launch, so route the operator to 60 pick a set first. 61 4. Echo the hot set (sprint · color) and **confirm before firing** — this spawns real terminal 62 windows, so a stale hot-flag shouldn't cost a fleet. The launcher then **excludes any hot sprint 63 already open in a tab** (*Skip-if-open* below), so mark those as skip in the echo and fire only the 64 rest. 65 5. On the operator's go, launch one session per hot sprint via the launcher below. 66 67 ## `/hot-start set` — curate, then launch on request 68 69 The editor for `HOT?` / `Color`. It reads and writes only those two keys. It does not fire on its own 70 — but once the set looks right, the operator can tell it to hot-start ("go", "hot start", "fire 71 them"), and it runs the launch sequence below (echo → confirm → launcher). Bare `/hot-start` launches 72 directly, skipping the editing step. 73 74 1. Glob the live specs as above (normalizing missing/blank `Color` to `#000000`, no `updated` bump). 75 Let **L** = count. 76 - **L ≤ 15** → show them all; don't bother reading `updated`. 77 - **L > 15** → read each spec's `updated` (fallback to the sibling `_CURSOR_`'s `updated`), sort 78 descending, and show the 15 most recent. 79 2. Display a table, **hot rows first, then the rest**. Hot rows always surface (they're the set you're 80 grooming); the recency window applies to the non-hot remainder. The leftmost **`#`** is a throwaway 81 row index for the current render only — not tied to any spec and never persisted — so the operator 82 can act by number ("add 2 and 5") instead of typing names; it renumbers every time the table redraws. 83 84 | # | HOT? | Sprint | Project | Color | Last updated | 85 |---|------|--------|---------|-------|--------------| 86 87 3. The operator drives it in natural language (by name or by the current `#`): 88 - **add `<#/sprint…>`** → set `HOT?: Yes`. The sprint keeps its `Color` (the default `#000000` if 89 you've never set one); offer a distinguishing color (hex or natural-language → hex), but a 90 default-black tab is a fine resting state. 91 - **remove `<#/sprint…>`** → set `HOT?: No`. 92 - **recolor `<#/sprint> `** → update `Color` (hex, or natural-language → hex). 93 - **show older** (only when L > 15) → display the next recency batch. 94 - **launch** ("go" / "hot start" / "fire them") → run the `/hot-start` launch sequence on the 95 current hot set (echo → confirm → exclude already-open sprints → fire). 96 4. **Writes touch only the `HOT?` / `Color` frontmatter keys** — add them if the spec lacks them. 97 Never edit the operator-authored Problem Description or any other spec section. (The `Color` 98 normalization to the default is the one write that can happen without an explicit edit — and it 99 leaves `updated` alone.) 100 5. After each edit, re-show the table and wait. Launch only when the operator asks. 101 102 ## The launcher 103 104 Launch **directly** — no generated `.ps1`, no `$env:LOCALAPPDATA\HotStart\runs\` file, no `schtasks`. 105 Hot-start fires *now*, so the loop runs inline in the launching session: one `wt.exe` call per hot 106 spec, **30 seconds apart**. `$Rows` is one entry per **hot** spec: 107 108 ```powershell 109 $Repo = 'C:\Users\alder\Desktop\[REDACTED:project]' 110 $Rows = @( # one entry per HOT spec 111 @{ Project='System Building'; Sprint='Hot Start'; Color='#009999' } 112 ) 113 114 # --- Skip-if-open: a hot-start tab's title IS its sprint name (--title + 115 # --suppressApplicationTitle), so a live Windows Terminal tab named after a 116 # hot sprint means it's already up. ---
name: launch-session
description: Open a new, top-level (non-child) interactive Claude Code session in its own Windows Terminal tab, seeded with one prompt. Use to hand work over to a fresh session, e.g. when this session is about to end or its context is degraded and HANDOVER.md says where to continue.
argument-hint: "<prompt> [working dir] [tab title]"
---

# Launch session

> Adapted by the assistant on 2026-10-15 from the operator's `hot-start` skill (`C:\Users\alder\Desktop\[REDACTED:project]\.claude\skills\hot-start\SKILL.md`): same `wt.exe` new-tab launch and the same four-variable env scrub, reduced to one session with a free prompt. Not yet run from this harness.

## When

- Only to continue work that is written down in a handover file the new session can read (for the overnight experiment: `System/Brainstorms/Experiments/2026-10-15/HANDOVER.md`).
- One session at a time. Before launching, make sure this session will stop working on the same steps (commit, tick the handover, then stop), so two sessions never work the same checklist.
- Not to fan out work; use subagents or workflows for that.

## Launch (PowerShell tool)

```powershell
$Dir    = 'C:\Users\alder\Desktop\Harness seed\.claude\worktrees\brainstorming-intent-pipelines'   # or the argument
$Title  = 'Handover'                                                                                 # or the argument
$Prompt = 'Read System/Brainstorms/Experiments/2026-10-15/HANDOVER.md and continue from the first unchecked step.'
$scrub = @(
  'set','CLAUDE_CODE_CHILD_SESSION=&',   # the determinant: a child marker stops the new session writing its own transcript
  'set','CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID=&',
  'set','CLAUDECODE=&',
  'set','CLAUDE_CODE_ENTRYPOINT=&'
)
$a = @('-w','0','new-tab','--suppressApplicationTitle','--title',$Title,'-d',$Dir,'cmd','/k') + $scrub + @('claude',$Prompt)
& wt.exe @a      # splat: PowerShell quotes each argument, so the prompt stays one token
```

- `set VAR=&` with the `&` glued to the value clears the variable (a space before `&` would store a space).
- `cmd /k` keeps the tab open after the session exits, so its scrollback survives.
- The new session starts in the operator's default permission mode. If that mode asks for permission, the session waits for him at the first prompt; choosing a mode that does not ask is the operator's decision, not this skill's.

## After launching

- Say in this session's chat that a new session was launched, with its title and prompt.
- Add a line to the handover log.

- Not to fan out work; use subagents or workflows for that.

## Launch (PowerShell tool)

```powershell
$Dir    = 'C:\Users\alder\Desktop\Harness seed\.claude\worktrees\brainstorming-intent-pipelines'   # or the argument
$Title  = 'Handover'                                                                                 # or the argument
$Prompt = 'Read System/Brainstorms/Experiments/2026-10-15/HANDOVER.md and continue from the first unchecked step.'
$scrub = @(
  'set','CLAUDE_CODE_CHILD_SESSION=&',   # the determinant: a child marker stops the new session writing its own transcript
  'set','CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID=&',
  'set','CLAUDECODE=&',
  'set','CLAUDE_CODE_ENTRYPOINT=&'
)
$a = @('-w','0','new-tab','--suppressApplicationTitle','--title',$Title,'-d',$Dir,'cmd','/k') + $scrub + @('claude',$Prompt)
& wt.exe @a      # splat: PowerShell quotes each argument, so the prompt stays one token
```

- `set VAR=&` with the `&` glued to the value clears the variable (a space before `&` would store a space).
- `cmd /k` keeps the tab open after the session exits, so its scrollback survives.
- The new session starts in the operator's default permission mode. If that mode asks for permission, the session waits for him at the first prompt; choosing a mode that does not ask is the operator's decision, not this skill's.

## After launching

- Say in this session's chat that a new session was launched, with its title and prompt.
- Add a line to the handover log.

"""Join blind judge scores, the blind map, the answer key and cost metrics into per-run and per-pipeline tables.

usage: aggregate.py <judge_result.json> <blind map.json> <answer key.json> <metrics.json> <out.json>
"""
import json, sys
from collections import defaultdict

judged = json.load(open(sys.argv[1], encoding="utf-8"))
mapping = json.load(open(sys.argv[2], encoding="utf-8"))
key = json.load(open(sys.argv[3], encoding="utf-8"))
metrics = json.load(open(sys.argv[4], encoding="utf-8"))

rows = []
for j in judged:
    if not j:
        continue
    run = mapping[j["code"]]["run"]
    n = len(key[j["q"]]["elements"])
    scores = [s for s in (j.get("opus"), j.get("fable")) if s]
    if not scores:
        continue
    cov = sum((len(set(s["elements_hit"])) + 0.5 * len(set(s["elements_partial"]) - set(s["elements_hit"]))) / n for s in scores) / len(scores)
    avg = lambda f: sum(s[f] for s in scores) / len(scores)
    m = metrics[run]
    rows.append({"run": run, "pipeline": run.split("_")[1], "mode": run.split("_")[2], "q": j["q"],
                 "coverage": round(cov, 2), "precision": avg("precision"), "detail": avg("detail"),
                 "unknowns": avg("unknowns"), "overall": avg("overall"),
                 "invented": sum(len(s["invented"]) for s in scores) / len(scores),
                 "words": m["words_shown"], "ticks": m["ticks"], "rounds": m["rounds"], "verdict": m["final_verdict"],
                 "judge_gap": abs(scores[0]["overall"] - scores[-1]["overall"])})

rows.sort(key=lambda r: (r["mode"], r["pipeline"], r["q"]))
print(f"{'run':22s} cov  prec det unk  ovr  inv words ticks verdict  gap")
for r in rows:
    print(f"{r['run']:22s}{r['coverage']:.2f} {r['precision']:4.1f}{r['detail']:4.1f}{r['unknowns']:4.1f}{r['overall']:5.1f}{r['invented']:5.1f}{r['words']:6d}{r['ticks']:6d}  {r['verdict']:7s}{r['judge_gap']:4.1f}")

by = defaultdict(list)
for r in rows:
    by[(r["pipeline"], r["mode"])].append(r)
print()
print(f"{'pipeline/mode':16s} cov  ovr  words  cov per 1k words")
summary = {}
for (p, mode), rs in sorted(by.items()):
    cov = sum(r["coverage"] for r in rs) / len(rs)
    ovr = sum(r["overall"] for r in rs) / len(rs)
    words = sum(r["words"] for r in rs) / len(rs)
    eff = cov / (words / 1000)
    summary[f"{p}_{mode}"] = {"coverage": round(cov, 2), "overall": round(ovr, 1), "words": round(words), "coverage_per_1k_words": round(eff, 3)}
    print(f"{p + '/' + mode:16s}{cov:.2f} {ovr:4.1f} {words:6.0f}  {eff:.3f}")
json.dump({"rows": rows, "summary": summary}, open(sys.argv[5], "w", encoding="utf-8"), indent=1)

# Results A (invented answer key, simulated operator)

Written by the assistant on 2026-10-15. One run per cell, a simulated operator (Sonnet 5.5) holding an answer key invented by Fable 5.1, two blind judges (Opus 5.5, Fable 5.1; they agreed within 1 point on 12 of 15). Treat as signals, not proof. Full numbers: `scores_A.json`, `metrics_A.json`, `judges_A.json`.

| Pipeline | Coverage attentive | Overall attentive | Words read attentive | Ticks | Coverage tired |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| P1 lens cards (operator's design) | 0.68 | 5.0 | 3.2k | 22 | 0.47 |
| P2 draft + claims | 0.64 | 5.5 | 4.6k | 29 | 0.55 |
| P3 best / worst | **0.77** | **6.1** | 3.5k | **9** | 0.40 |
| P4 decision forks | 0.56 | 5.2 | **2.2k** | 9 | 0.35 |
| P5 hybrid | 0.70 | 5.2 | 3.2k | 20 | **0.70** |

Coverage = share of the key's intent elements a judge could read off the final INTENT.md (partial = half).

## Findings

1. **Best/worst (P3) recovered the most intent per click**: 9 ticks for 0.77 coverage with an attentive operator.
2. **Only the hybrid (P5) survived "yeah, fine".** With the tired operator, P5 kept 0.70 coverage; the rest fell to 0.35-0.55. P5 is the only pipeline whose forks and claims force a choice between contradicting options.
3. **Precision is the weakest score everywhere (about 3-6.5 of 10).** Every final intent stated about five commitments as the operator's that he never made: assistant guesses written as decisions. This is the over-generalisation failure from SNIP_2026-10-14_231927.
4. **Confirming a ~300-word INTENT.md never succeeded.** All ten attentive runs hit their round cap at "Close". The confirmation step is too large for Operator RAM and keeps finding one more gap.
5. **Reading load is dominated by INTENT rounds**, not by the cards, forks or picks.

## Changes to test in experiment B

- INTENT.md states only points the operator ticked or wrote; everything else goes under "Still open". Judges count invented commitments.
- Confirmation by at most 8 one-line claims (yes / no), not by reading the whole INTENT.md.
- Every pipeline gets P5's anti-"yeah fine" device: options that contradict each other, so ticking everything high is visibly inconsistent.
- Candidates: P3 with claim confirmation; P5 with claim confirmation; one new pipeline the B session designs from these findings.

Build (parallel implementation).** Modules built in parallel per the design, each with unit tests against mocks: idea intake, landing page generator, registrar/DNS, email infrastructure, lead generation, outreach copy, sending/warm-up, metrics, PMF scoring (Jev), portfolio + budget scheduler, compliance, hand-off queue. content.text:
PMF phase 1 is done: 14 agents, no errors. Its answer to your captcha question:

- **For the recurring work, it's a solved problem.** Domains, DNS, hosting, lead scraping, verification, sending, metrics and Jev all run on API keys with no captchas.
- **Captchas sit only at one-time account signups** (Porkbun and Google Workspace are documented; the others are unverified). Solvers exist, but those services' terms forbid bot signups, so each signup becomes one human step. That makes it neither hard nor impossible.

The critic also found five gaps for the design to cover:

- Nothing yet turns an idea into a target customer profile, lead queries and email copy.
- Nobody handles replies.
- Czech law needs consent, so Czech recipients are blocked by default.
- The research gives conflicting reply-rate thresholds for what counts as a pass.
- No domain-purchase route has been chosen.

Committing, then launching phase 2: three architecture proposals judged by two models.

The pipeline redesign is done. The judges ranked the three designs 65, 61 and 57 and found faults in all of them; the writer fixed those in the top two:

- **P6, tensions and claims:** short readings with best/worst picks, A/B tension files with a "your call, stays open" option, then claims files of at most 8 lines. Each claims file contains a mirror pair, two lines that contradict each other, so "Yes" on both voids every "Yes" in that file.
- **P7, ticked ledger:** a running record of ticks, and the final intent is built only from rows you confirmed with a "Yes" in a file that passed its contradiction check. There's a final check step.
- **Contract B:** only points you ticked or wrote count as yours, each tagged with its source. Files are capped at 250 words and rounds at 350.

Committing these, then launching experiment B. P6 and P7 run under contract B. P3 and P5, the winners from A, run as controls under the original contract. All four face a simulated operator who holds your real intent.

input.content:
# Results B (real intent, simulated operator)

Written by the assistant on 2026-10-15. The simulated operator (Sonnet 5.5) held the operator's real intent for the captcha questions (his own words in SNIP_2026-10-15_014914; elements derived by the assistant). Two blind judges (Opus 5.5, Fable 5.1) agreed within 1 point on 14 of 16. One run per cell; signals, not proof. Numbers: `scores_B.json`, `metrics_B.json`, `judges_B.json`. "Words" = words in files the operator must tick.

| Pipeline | Coverage attentive | Overall attentive | Coverage tired | Words attentive |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| P3 best / worst (contract A) | **0.53** | **5.0** | 0.21 | 3.5k |
| P5 hybrid (contract A) | 0.41 | 4.5 | **0.29** | 3.0k |
| P6 tensions + claims (contract B) | 0.27 | 3.5 | 0.18 | **1.1k** |
| P7 ticked ledger (contract B) | 0.26 | 3.0 | 0.18 | **1.0k** |

## Findings

1. **The real intent is mostly not recoverable by clicking.** Its core (the PMF-tester application, Jev for PMF scoring, many ideas with budgets, the high-velocity thesis) is information only the operator holds. No assistant-written reading contains it, so ticking readings cannot surface it. It entered the runs only when the simulated operator wrote it in a note.
2. **Experiment A overstated what pipelines can do.** Its answer key was written by a model, so other models could guess it. A human's intent is less guessable. Future tests need human answer keys (the operator's own words), as here.
3. **Cutting reading cut coverage.** P6 and P7 asked for a third of the reading of P3/P5 and recovered about half as much. The judge panel had predicted this ("coverage capped by design").
4. **Invented commitments persisted under contract B** (about 5 per intent). A simulated "Yes" on an assistant-written claim still counts as confirmed, so "only what he ticked" does not stop the assistant's framing becoming his.
5. **P3 (best/worst) won with an attentive operator in both experiments; P5 was the most robust with a tired one in both.** Neither is good enough alone.

## What this implies for the pipeline

- The single most valuable input is **one line from the operator on what the question is for** (the decision or project it feeds). It is cheap for him and carries what no reading can. Ask for it first, as an optional one-line fence, before any readings.
- Readings and claims are then for shaping and checking that line, not for discovering it.
- Measure precision with human answer keys only.

"""Coverage of a chosen subset of key elements (default 0,1,2), per pipeline/mode, from judge results and the blind map."""
import json, sys
from collections import defaultdict

judged = json.load(open(sys.argv[1], encoding="utf-8"))
mapping = json.load(open(sys.argv[2], encoding="utf-8"))
core = [int(x) for x in (sys.argv[3] if len(sys.argv) > 3 else "0,1,2").split(",")]
by = defaultdict(list)
for j in judged:
    run = mapping[j["code"]]["run"]
    scores = [s for s in (j.get("opus"), j.get("fable")) if s]
    vals = []
    for s in scores:
        hit = set(s["elements_hit"]); part = set(s["elements_partial"]) - hit
        vals.append(sum(1 if e in hit else 0.5 if e in part else 0 for e in core) / len(core))
    p, mode = run.split("_")[1], run.split("_")[2]
    by[(p, mode)].append(sum(vals) / len(vals))
for (p, mode), v in sorted(by.items()):
    print(f"{p}/{mode:10s} core coverage {sum(v)/len(v):.2f}  (n={len(v)})")

  name: 'pmf-integrate',
  description: 'PMF tester phase 4: integrate, end-to-end dry run, three adversarial audits, fix, re-verify',
  phases: [{ title: 'Integrate' }, { title: 'Audit' }, { title: 'Fix' }],
}
const PMF = 'C:/Users/alder/Desktop/Harness seed/.claude/worktrees/brainstorming-intent-pipelines/Work/PMF-tester'
const TEST = `cd "${PMF}" && python -m unittest discover -s tests -t .`
const RULES = `Hard rules (${PMF}/BUILD_PLAN.md): no real side effects; no network, subprocess or vendor call may run; dry_run stays the default; no credentials; no captcha solving; compliance gates mandatory. Stdlib only, no package installs. Do not run git. Keep runtime state under var/ (gitignored).`
phase('Integrate')
const integ = await agent(`You are the integrator of the PMF tester (Python). Read ${PMF}/DESIGN.md, ${PMF}/BUILD_PLAN.md, and every file in ${PMF}/notes/ (interface requests from module agents). ${RULES}
1. Resolve each interface request (edit shared core or modules as needed, keeping all tests green). Record what you did at the end of each notes file.
2. Make the end-to-end dry run work through the real CLI: three sample ideas from ${PMF}/ideas/sample_ideas.toml, each with a budget, running through every lifecycle state over simulated weeks (the sim module), with all vendors mocked, hand-offs raised and answered by a scripted simulated operator, and a PMF likelihood per idea at the end plus a portfolio summary. Add an e2e test for it.
3. Write ${PMF}/README.md: what the tool does, the exact commands to run the dry run on Windows, where output goes, what is mocked vs real, and the hand-offs a real run would ask of the operator. Plain words, short.
4. Run ${TEST} until green. Return: the dry-run command, its final summary output (max 40 lines), test count, and what you changed (max 120 words).`, { label: 'integrate', phase: 'Integrate', effort: 'high' })
phase('Audit')
const LENSES = [
  { key: 'safety', p: 'SAFETY: try hard to find any path to a real side effect: network sockets, urllib/http/ssl imports reachable at runtime, subprocess, os.system, webbrowser, SDK imports, environment variables (e.g. a TYPESAFE_API_KEY or vendor key set in the environment flipping a real client on), live-guard bypasses, dry_run defaults that can be overridden by config without an explicit operator flag, file writes outside var/. Prove each finding with a file:line and a concrete scenario.' },
  { key: 'correctness', p: 'CORRECTNESS: run the end-to-end dry run yourself and inspect its outputs and state. Check: every idea reaches a terminal state; budgets never exceeded; compliance gates block what DESIGN.md says (CZ recipients blocked by default, suppression and unsubscribe honoured); hand-offs block only what they should; resuming after an interrupted tick does not double any spend or send; the PMF score is computed from the metrics as designed. Prove findings with commands and output.' },
  { key: 'operator_ram', p: 'OPERATOR RAM: the operator has very low working memory. Read every hand-off prompt, status output and report the tool shows a human (run the dry run and the status/handoff commands). Flag anything that needs more than a short read to act on, requires cross-referencing, or is ambiguous. Give the exact text and a shorter replacement.' },
]
const FIND = { type: 'object', properties: { findings: { type: 'array', items: { type: 'object', properties: { severity: { type: 'string', enum: ['critical', 'major', 'minor'] }, where: { type: 'string' }, what: { type: 'string' }, fix: { type: 'string' } }, required: ['severity', 'where', 'what', 'fix'] } } }, required: ['findings'] }
const audits = (await parallel(LENSES.map(l => () => agent(`Adversarially audit the PMF tester at ${PMF} (read DESIGN.md and README.md first). Integrator's report:\n${integ}\n\n${l.p}\nDo not modify files. Return findings (empty list if none survive your own scrutiny).`, { label: `audit:${l.key}`, phase: 'Audit', effort: 'high', schema: FIND })))).filter(Boolean)
const all = audits.flatMap((a, i) => a.findings.map(f => ({ lens: LENSES[i].key, ...f })))
log(`${all.length} findings: ${all.filter(f => f.severity === 'critical').length} critical, ${all.filter(f => f.severity === 'major').length} major`)
phase('Fix')
const fixed = all.length ? await agent(`Fix these audit findings in the PMF tester at ${PMF}. First verify each one (reproduce it); fix those that are real, starting with critical; skip and explain any that are not real. ${RULES}\nRun ${TEST} until green and re-run the end-to-end dry run. Append a "Verification" section to ${PMF}/README.md listing each finding with fixed / not real / deferred and one line why.\n\nFindings:\n${JSON.stringify(all, null, 1)}\n\nReturn: counts fixed / not real / deferred, final test count, and the deferred items.`, { label: 'fix', phase: 'Fix', effort: 'high' }) : 'no findings'
return { integrate: integ, findings: all.map(f => `${f.lens}/${f.severity}: ${f.what.slice(0, 160)}`), fixed }

  name: 'pmf-baseline-report',
  description: 'PMF tester phase 5: collect every intent guess from design, code, config and notes; completeness critic; BASELINE_REPORT.md',

}
const ROOT = 'C:/Users/alder/Desktop/Harness seed/.claude/worktrees/brainstorming-intent-pipelines'
const PMF = ROOT + '/Work/PMF-tester'
const GUESS = { type: 'object', properties: { guesses: { type: 'array', items: { type: 'object', properties: { topic: { type: 'string' }, guess: { type: 'string', description: 'what the build assumed, one sentence' }, where: { type: 'string', description: 'file:line or setting' }, impact: { type: 'string', enum: ['high', 'medium', 'low'] }, question: { type: 'string', description: 'the one short question the operator could answer to settle it' } }, required: ['topic', 'guess', 'where', 'impact', 'question'] } } }, required: ['guesses'] }
const SOURCES = [

  { key: 'config_code', p: `${PMF}/config/pmft.toml, ${PMF}/ideas/sample_ideas.toml, and defaults hard-coded in ${PMF}/src/pmft/ (thresholds, budgets, send volumes, warm-up length, pass bars, scoring priors, country lists, copy tone, hand-off wording). Grep for constants and default= values.` },
  { key: 'notes_readme', p: `${PMF}/README.md (Verification section, deferred items), every file in ${PMF}/notes/, and ${PMF}/research/STEP_MAP.md (unverified items that a design decision rests on)` },
]
phase('Collect')
const found = (await parallel(SOURCES.map(s => () => agent(`The PMF tester was built as a baseline experiment from the operator's intent as stated in ${ROOT}/System/Snippets/SNIP_2026-10-15_014914.md (section 3) with NO further clarification. Find every point where the build had to guess what the operator wants (a choice his words do not settle: product, business, compliance, budget, workflow, UX, tooling). Source to scan: ${s.p}. Read the snippet first so you can tell what he did state. Do not list pure engineering choices that do not depend on his intent. Return the guesses.`, { label: `collect:${s.key}`, phase: 'Collect', effort: 'high', schema: GUESS })))).filter(Boolean)
const all = found.flatMap(f => f.guesses)
log(`${all.length} raw guesses`)
phase('Critic')
const critic = await agent(`Completeness critic. ${all.length} intent guesses were collected from the PMF tester at ${PMF} (list below). Read the operator's spec ${ROOT}/System/Snippets/SNIP_2026-10-15_014914.md and walk his chain step by step (idea in, landing page, domain, DNS, Workspace + DKIM/SPF, Apify leads, cold email copy, sending service, warm-up, sending, metrics after N emails, Jev PMF probability, many ideas with budgets over weeks, users outside GTM). For each step, check the code and config for decisions that depend on his intent but are missing from the list. Return only the missing ones.\n\n${JSON.stringify(all.map(g => g.topic + ': ' + g.guess))}`, { label: 'critic', phase: 'Critic', effort: 'high', schema: GUESS })
const merged = all.concat(critic.guesses)
phase('Report')
const report = await agent(`Write ${PMF}/BASELINE_REPORT.md. Purpose: the PMF tester was built as a baseline from the operator's stated intent with no further clarification; this report measures how far that got and what intent was missing. Audience: the operator, who has very low Operator RAM, and future sessions. Refer to "the operator", not "you".

Structure:
1. "In short" (max 6 lines): what works (dry run end to end on mocks; cite numbers from ${PMF}/README.md and ${PMF}/BUILD_PLAN.md), what is not real, the captcha answer (from ${PMF}/research/STEP_MAP.md, one sentence), and how many intent guesses were needed and how many are high impact.
2. "The 10 questions that matter most": the highest-impact guesses, deduplicated, each as one yes/no or pick-one question the operator can answer in a few words, with the build's current guess shown as the default.
3. "What a one-line purpose would have settled" vs "what needs the operator's own knowledge": split the guesses into those the intent pipeline could have surfaced cheaply and those only he can supply.
4. "All guesses": a table (topic | guess | where | impact), deduplicated, grouped by chain step.
5. "Real vs mocked": one line per vendor.
6. "Before any live run": the operator decisions and accounts needed (the hand-off list), and the deferred finding.
Keep sections 1-2 within one screen. Plain words.

Guesses (raw, may overlap):\n${JSON.stringify(merged, null, 1)}\n\nReturn section 1 and section 2 exactly as written.`, { label: 'report', phase: 'Report', effort: 'high' })
return { raw: all.length, critic_added: critic.guesses.length, report }

lines: +description: Launch a new, independent, interactive Claude Code session in its own visible PowerShell window, from inside a running session, optionally with a first message already typed in. Use when the operator says "open a new session in <folder>", "launch a session", "start a fresh session for this", "hand this off to a new session", "kick off <task> in a new window", or "/new-local-session". The new session is a peer (transcript saved, resumable, visible to other sessions), not a nested child, and the operator can watch and talk to it.
+Launch a new, independent, top-level Claude Code session in its own PowerShell window.
+Check the argument against this list **first**. A clear match needs no filesystem search:

+The list is a shortcut, not a whitelist. Desktop holds both `[REDACTED:project]` and `alderman ai`, plus `[REDACTED:project]` and `[REDACTED:project]`, so a bare "alderman" or "alderman ai" is **ambiguous** and goes to the search.
+**If no directory is given, ask the operator which one.** Use `AskUserQuestion` with the first three rows as options. Don't default to the current directory or guess.
+If a directory is given, treat it as descriptive, not a strict path:
+1. Matches a **Common targets** row: use that path.
+2. Already an existing absolute path (`Test-Path`): use it verbatim.
+4. Nothing found: retry on each word separately (a folder matching all words beats one matching some), then one level deeper under Desktop.
+Exactly one match: use it. More than one: `AskUserQuestion` with the full paths. None: say so and ask. Never invent a path.

+**Start at the project root.** Claude Code reads project settings (`.claude/settings.json`, `settings.local.json`, project hooks) from the folder a session starts in, not from the repository root. A session started in a sub-folder loses them (it still loads root skills). If the operator names a sub-folder of a repo, launch at the repo root and put the sub-folder in the first message instead.
+If the operator wants the new session to start on a task, write the message to a UTF-8 text file:
+- **No double quotes anywhere in the text.** Use single quotes or none. Windows PowerShell 5.1 mangles double quotes inside arguments it passes to `claude.exe`.

+Run this, with the resolved path in `Set-Location` and, if there is a first message, its file path in `Get-Content`. Set `dangerouslyDisableSandbox: true` on the tool call; spawning a detached window is blocked under the sandbox.

+$inner = 'foreach ($v in ''CLAUDE_CODE_CHILD_SESSION'',''CLAUDECODE'',''CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID'',''CLAUDE_JOB_DIR'',''CLAUDE_PID'',''CLAUDE_EFFORT'',''CLAUDE_CODE_BRIDGE_SESSION_ID'',''CLAUDE_CODE_MESSAGING_SOCKET'',''CLAUDE_CODE_MESSAGING_TOKEN'',''CLAUDE_CODE_AGENT'',''CLAUDE_CODE_ENTRYPOINT'',''CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ATTENDED'',''CLAUDE_CODE_ALT_SCREEN_FULL_REPAINT'',''NO_COLOR'',''FORCE_COLOR'',''AI_AGENT'',''GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT'') { Remove-Item -Path (''Env:'' + $v) -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue }; $env:CLAUDE_CODE_FORCE_SESSION_PERSISTENCE = ''1''; Set-Location ''<RESOLVED PATH>''; claude'
+# With a first message, end $inner with this instead of the bare claude:
+Why it's built this way, so it doesn't get "improved" into something broken:

+- **Every shell a session runs inherits that session's markers.** A `claude` started from it counts as nested: no transcript, not resumable, invisible to `claude agents`, FleetView and cross-session messaging. The loop removes the markers. `CLAUDE_CODE_FORCE_SESSION_PERSISTENCE=1` is the documented override that forces persistence and registration anyway. It's a second safeguard in case a new marker appears in a later version.

+- **The tool shell's own settings are stripped too.** `CLAUDE_CODE_ALT_SCREEN_FULL_REPAINT` is documented as switched on automatically for background sessions on Windows. `NO_COLOR`, `FORCE_COLOR`, `AI_AGENT` and `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT` are injected into tool shells according to a community report (GitHub #82825); the docs don't mention them. Inherited, `NO_COLOR` makes the new session render without color (observed 2026-10-09: grey mascot, colorless UI), and `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0` would stop git from asking for credentials. The colorless UI is the visible sign that inheritance happened.
+- **`CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ATTENDED` is stripped** so a launch from a background session doesn't pass on "unattended". The new session is attended; the operator is looking at it.

+- **Never put double quotes inside `$inner`.** `Start-Process` passes it through the Windows native command-line parser, which strips unescaped double quotes. An assignment like `$env:X="false"` arrives as `$env:X=false`, `false` runs as a command, throws, and the assignment silently never happens. That's how an earlier version of this skill failed invisibly (verified 2026-08-25). Quote with doubled single quotes (`''1''`, `''<path>''`), which survive.
+- **Remove rather than set to 0.** Removal doesn't depend on how each variable's value is parsed.
+- `-NoExit` keeps the window open. `Start-Process` detaches it.
+- **Never** run `claude` in the foreground of this session; it will hang. **Never** `Set-Location` this session into the target; only the child moves.
+- **Process:** a `claude.exe` created seconds ago whose parent is the new `powershell.exe`. None means the launch failed: report it, don't silently retry.
+- **Registration:** `Test-Path` must be `True`. `False` means a marker leaked and the session is running suppressed. Say so and stop.

+- **Transcript (when a first message was passed):** within about 10 seconds a new `.jsonl` appears under `~/.claude/projects/<munged-cwd>/` (non-alphanumerics in the path become `-`) and contains the message's first line. Check with `Select-String -SimpleMatch`.
+If the operator reports `Transcript saving is off — inherited CLAUDE_CODE_CHILD_SESSION marker`, or a colorless UI, the launch went wrong regardless of what this step said.

+Use `--bg` only when the operator asks for a session that runs without a window. For a session they want to watch and talk to, it's the wrong tool (Claude Code docs, agent view and worktrees pages, read 2026-10-09, v2.1.295):
+- **Not visible** until someone runs `claude attach <name>` or opens `claude agents`. Questions and permission prompts wait under "Needs input" until then.

+- **Edits land somewhere else.** Before editing, it moves into a git worktree under `.claude/worktrees/`, so changes don't appear in the working copy or in Obsidian. The exception is a project that sets `worktree.bgIsolation: "none"`.
+- **It commits and pushes without asking** in that worktree (never to main, never force-pushes).
+- **It runs as "background job · unattended"** in `/status` when nobody is attached. The docs don't say what else that changes in Claude's behaviour.
+- **Trust comes first.** The folder must have been trusted interactively; from a script it exits with "Workspace not trusted".
+- **It's a research preview.** Agent view has had frequent Windows fixes (a stale `daemon.lock` blocking every start, the keyboard not responding, sessions reopening with "no saved transcript").
+What `--bg` is good for: work that has to outlive the terminal, sessions resumed later from agent view, and runs nobody needs to watch.

+Policy check, same date: Anthropic's support article (support.claude.com/en/articles/15036540, Oct 7, 2026 update) says Max subscriptions can still be used for the Agent SDK, `claude -p` and third-party apps, and now include monthly API credits. Nothing official treats a session launched by another session differently from one started by hand.
+**On success, the entire user-facing output for this skill is one line:**
+Nothing else. The operator can see the window. This overrides any habit of ending with a summary.
+**On any problem the terseness rule is off.** Report what failed, the actual output, and what it means for the new session. Never dress a failure up as `Verification: ✅`.
